newsitem.title: turkmenistan: Investors welcome Turkmen oil law, but remain wary.
newsitem.headline: Investors welcome Turkmen oil law, but remain wary.

text.p: Turkmenistan took a major step towards attracting foreign money to tap huge energy reserves by signing a petroleum law last week, but more has to be done to protect nervous investors, Western energy executives said on Wednesday.

The former Soviet republic wants international energy firms to invest in ageing infrastructure, develop untapped resources and provide export outlets in the hope they will reverse a steep decline in oil and gas production since independence in 1991.

"The economy of Turkmenistan depends heavily on the oil and gas industry ... and the President is pursuing a so-called 'open doors' policy," Oil and Gas Minister Gochmurad Nazdjanov told the Turkmenistan International Oil and Gas Projects Conference.

He said a tender for exploration rights to around six blocks of Turkmenistan's section of the Caspian Sea was the next major step towards enticing outside funding to the cash-strapped, but resource-rich, Central Asian country.
"This development will need major investment. We've done a lot of work to ensure the security of the foreign investor," he said.
On Tuesday Nazdjanov said a petroleum law had come into force providing the legal basis for foreign investment in oil, which many executives saw as a test case for investment in all sectors.
It set out the broad terms under which companies can enter joint ventures with the state, while leaving room for negotiation.

"I think the legislation is evidence of the improving environment," said John Pek, managing director of Petronas Carigali Turkmenistan, a unit of Malaysia's state-owned Petronas which has a production-sharing agreement with Turkmenistan. "It is a quantum leap forward."
Lawyers agreed that the legislation signified progress in what has often proved to be a murky and fickle investment climate, but added that more work needed to be done.
"The legislation gives a lot of room for negotiations. But ... some sections are ambiguous, for example arbitration," said Andrei Yakovlev, corporate lawyer at McKenna and Co International.
Some potential investors questioned whether major discoveries would be made at all in the planned offshore tender, despite upbeat comments from government officials.

"It is too early to say that there is nothing out there, but there may well not be massive structures," said Alan Weatherill of Shell EP International Ventures BV, part of the Royal Dutch/Shell group. "We also feel things are a little overpriced," he added.
